title: Genesis 13. The Cup Shared.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 13. The Cup Shared.
Abram goes up from Egypt.
He comes out with his wife, all that he had,
and Lot with him.
He is very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.
The Cup that was endangered in Egypt, traded for livestock,
handed to a foreign king, has been returned with interest.
What Abram lost by fear, God restored by intervention.
The wealth of Pharaoh's house has followed the man God preserved.
He returns to the South, traveling by stages back to Bethel,
to the place where his tent was at the beginning,
between Bethel and Ai.
To the place of the altar he had made there at first.
There Abram called on the name of the Lord.
He goes back to where he started.
The man who went down to Egypt returns to the altar he built before the famine.
The Cup that was carried into Egypt is brought back to the place of worship.
Lot also, who went with Abram, has flocks and herds and tents.
The land cannot bear both of them.
Their possessions are so great that they cannot live together.
Strife breaks out between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock.
The Canaanites and the Perizzites are dwelling in the land.
The Cup that was shared is now too full.
The vessel that held two families cannot hold them both.
And the conflict is happening in front of the people God promised the land to,
Canaanites and Perizzites who have not yet been displaced.
The witness to the promise is watching the promise's heirs quarrel over grass.
Abram, the elder, the one who received the calling,
the one who holds the covenant, speaks to Lot:
Let there be no strife between you and me,
and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen.
Is not the whole land before you?
Separate yourself from me.
If you take the left hand, I will go to the right.
If you take the right hand, I will go to the left.
The man who grabbed in Egypt,
who seized safety by giving away his wife,
now gives away the choice.
The elder yields to the younger.
The one who holds the promise offers the promise's land to the one who does not.
This is not weakness.
It is the first act of restraint in Abram's story.
The Cup that was given is not grabbed.
It is opened.
Lot lifts up his eyes.
He sees all the plain of the Jordan, well-watered everywhere.
Before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah,
it was like the garden of the Lord,
like the land of Egypt, as you go toward Zoar.
Lot sees the garden.
The text names it: like the garden of the Lord.
The same phrase used for Eden.
The water, the fertility, the abundance,
the Cup that was emptied in chapter three and refilled in chapter eight is visible again in the plain of Jordan.
But the text also marks the end:
before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.
The garden that Lot sees is already sentenced.
The reader knows what Lot does not.
Lot chooses.
He takes the plain of the Jordan for himself.
He travels east.
They separate from one another.
Abram dwells in the land of Canaan.
Lot dwells in the cities of the plain and moves his tent as far as Sodom.
Lot chose the water, not the people.
He saw abundance and did not ask who lived in it.
He saw the garden and did not ask what grew there.
He moved toward Sodom, and the text stops to note:
Now the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the Lord.
The Cup that was shared has been divided.
Lot took the better land and walked toward the worse people.
Abram took the less and stayed in the land God promised.
After Lot separated from him, the Lord spoke to Abram.
The timing is exact.
God speaks after the division is complete.
The Cup that was shared with Lot is now given entirely to Abram,
but only after Abram gave the choice away.
The man who did not grab received what the man who grabbed could not hold.
Lift up your eyes.
Look from the place where you are, northward, southward, eastward, westward.
All the land that you see,
I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth.
If a man can count the dust of the earth,
then your offspring also can be counted.
The same gesture Lot just made, lifting up his eyes and seeing,
God now asks Abram to make.
But where Lot saw a plain that would be destroyed,
Abram is told to see a land that will be given.
Where Lot chose water, Abram is given dust.
The dust of the earth,
the same word used for Abram's own body in chapter three,
the dust God cursed and man was told he would return to,
is now the measure of his offspring.
What was a sign of death becomes a sign of multitude.
Arise.
Walk through the land, its length and its breadth,
for I will give it to you.
Abram is told to walk the land, not to build a tower,
not to make a name, not to gather a city.
To walk.
The man who was told to go now walks what he was given.
The Cup that was poured out in creation, scattered at Babel,
narrowed at Haran,
and endangered in Egypt is now placed under Abram's feet.
The promise is not a monument.
It is a path.
Abram moves his tent.
He comes to the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron,
and builds an altar there to the Lord.
God speaks.
Man worships.
The pattern holds.
The Cup is shared, then divided, then narrowed, then confirmed,
and the confirmation is always an altar.
Where God speaks, Abram builds.
Where the promise lands, worship rises.
The man who fumbled in Egypt is now the man who builds altars in Canaan.
Not because he changed.
Because the Cup holds.
Lot is in Sodom.
Abram is in Hebron.
The two men who shared one cup have separated.
One chose what his eyes could see.
The other was given what only God can see.
What each chose has not yet caught up with them.
But it will.
